mainTopic: Which animals have בכור status, mixed-species births, and following the mother's status
overview: The גמרא proves that among non-kosher animals, only a donkey has בכור status, not a horse or a camel. The first proof comes from the Torah writing ״פטר חמור״ twice. רב אחאי challenges it, and the גמרא defends it from the repeated word ״פטר״. Our משנה's תנא uses that repetition for something else, so רב פפא gives him a different source: a כלל ופרט in the verse. רבי יוסי הגלילי and the רבנן then argue over whether the donkey belongs in that list, based on the words ״ופטר״ and the letter ו׳. Next, the גמרא asks a ladder of questions about a mother that gives birth to an animal that looks like another species but has some of its mother's features. Two ברייתות show that a cow's donkey-like calf with some of the mother's features is a בכור, but the horse cases are not proven. Finally, the גמרא explains that for eating, an animal's status follows its mother, not its own looks. It begins bringing a verse for this rule, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The double phrase limits firstborn status to donkeys
steps.stepSummary: The Torah writes ״פטר חמור״ two times to teach that only firstborn donkeys, not horses or camels, have בכור status.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says "firstborn of a donkey," "firstborn of a donkey" — two times. This means: I told you about firstborn donkeys, and not about firstborn horses or camels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its source from the פסוק: because ״פטר חמור״ is written twice, the law of a firstborn non-kosher animal is limited to donkeys only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One mention of ״פטר חמור״ would already teach the basic law. The second mention looks extra, so the גמרא reads it as a limit: donkeys, and nothing else. Horses and camels are left out of בכור status completely.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse teaches (introduces a source from a פסוק)
The firstborn of a donkey
Two times
Horses and camels

phrases.english: The verse states:
"Firstborn of a donkey," "firstborn of a donkey" — two times
phrases.notes: The two places are שמות י״ג:י״ג and שמות ל״ד:כ׳.

phrases.english: I told you about firstborn donkeys,
and not about firstborn horses and camels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the derivation earlier, which asked whether horses and camels have בכור status.
steps.raayaObject: Only firstborn donkeys have בכור status; horses and camels do not.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The repetition of ״פטר חמור״ in שמות י״ג:י״ג and ל״ד:כ׳.

steps.title: רב אחאי explains why a second verse is needed anyway
steps.stepSummary: רב אחאי argues that with only one verse, the donkey would be read as an example that teaches about all non-kosher animals. So the second verse has a different job.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחאי objects: If the Torah had written it only once, I would have said: something that was part of a general group and was singled out to teach a rule was not singled out to teach only about itself. It was singled out to teach about the whole group. So really, every non-kosher animal would be redeemed with a lamb.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחאי begins his attack. He is setting up his challenge by showing that the second ״פטר חמור״ is needed for a different reason, so it cannot serve as the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule of דרשה: when one item is taken out of a larger group to teach a law, that law applies to the whole group. With just one verse, we would think every firstborn non-kosher animal is redeemed with a שה. A second verse is needed to block that idea, so the repetition is already used up.

keyTerms.meaning: Challenges, refutes
I would have thought

keyTerms.term: דָּבָר שֶׁהָיָה בַּכְּלָל וְיָצָא מִן הַכְּלָל
keyTerms.meaning: An item that was part of a general group and was singled out from it
To teach about the whole group
A lamb or kid used to redeem the firstborn donkey

steps.confusionAlert: רב אחאי is not arguing that horses and camels have בכור status. He is only saying the second verse may be needed for something else, so it does not prove they lack it.

phrases.english: Rav Achai refutes:
If the Merciful One had written it once,
I would have said
an item that was included in a general group,
and was singled out from the group to teach,
was not singled out to teach only about itself,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לְלַמֵּד עַל הַכְּלָל כּוּלּוֹ יָצָא,
phrases.english: but was singled out to teach about the entire group,
and so really, all would be redeemed with a lamb.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof in step 1 by giving the second verse a different job.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from the double ״פטר חמור״.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without a second verse, the donkey would teach about all non-kosher animals through the rule of דבר שהיה בכלל. So the second verse is needed to limit redemption with a שה to donkeys, not to remove בכור status.

steps.title: Maybe horses and camels are excluded only from lamb redemption
steps.stepSummary: רב אחאי finishes his challenge. The second verse may only remove horses and camels from redemption with a שה, while they still need redemption with any other item.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the Merciful One wrote "firstborn of a donkey" another time: firstborn donkeys, and not firstborn horses and camels. But say that it only excludes them from a lamb, and really they are redeemed with anything.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחאי finishes his question. The extra verse may exclude horses and camels only from the lamb, not from being a בכור at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second verse is now read narrowly. It tells us horses and camels are not redeemed with a שה. It may say nothing about whether they need redemption in some other way. So the proof from step 1 is not yet solid.

keyTerms.meaning: Another (a second time)
But I could say
He excluded them
With any item

phrases.english: So the Merciful One wrote "firstborn of a donkey" another time,

phrases.aramaic: פִּטְרֵי חֲמוֹרִים וְלֹא פִּטְרֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים,
phrases.english: to teach: firstborn donkeys, and not firstborn horses and camels,
but say: it excluded them from redemption with a lamb,
and really they are redeemed with any item!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב אחאי's challenge that began in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion that horses and camels have no בכור status.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The extra verse can be explained as removing only the lamb method. Horses and camels might still be בכורות that are redeemed with other items.

steps.title: The repeated word firstborn proves the limit is on firstborn status
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah only wanted to limit the lamb, it could have written ״חמור תפדה בשה״ the second time. Repeating ״פטר״ shows the limit is on firstborn status itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the Merciful One should have written: "Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb," and then "A donkey you shall redeem with a lamb." Why do I need "Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb" both times? To teach: I told you about firstborn donkeys, and not about firstborn horses and camels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב אחאי from the exact wording. The second verse repeats the word ״פטר״ (firstborn) even though it was not needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To limit the lamb to donkeys, the second verse only needed to say ״חמור תפדה בשה״. The extra word ״פטר״ must teach something more. It teaches that only a donkey's firstborn is a בכור at all. So the original proof stands: horses and camels have no בכור status.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Let the Merciful One write (the Torah should have written)
You shall redeem
Why do I need it?

steps.whatToRemember: Only a firstborn donkey has בכור status among non-kosher animals. The proof comes from the Torah repeating the word ״פטר״ in the second verse, which would have been unnecessary just to limit redemption with a שה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common method of the גמרא: it weighs the exact words of a פסוק. Even after one extra verse is explained, an extra word inside it can still teach a separate law.

phrases.english: If so, let the Merciful One write:
"Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb"
and "A donkey you shall redeem with a lamb."
phrases.notes: The second time without the word ״פטר״

phrases.aramaic: ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה״, ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה״
phrases.english: "Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb," "firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb" —
why do I need this?
I told you about firstborn donkeys,
and not about firstborn horses and camels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחאי's challenge from steps 2 and 3 and brings back the proof of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra-word analysis: the repeated word ״פטר״ goes beyond what the narrow reading needs.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second verse only limits redemption with a שה to donkeys, so horses and camels might still be בכורות redeemed with other items.
steps.terutzMaskana: The repeated ״פטר״ limits בכור status itself to donkeys. Horses and camels are not בכורות at all.

steps.title: Where does our משנה's תנא learn to exclude horses and camels?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the תנא of our משנה knows that horses and camels have no בכור status, since he used the repeated ״פטר חמור״ for a different law.
steps.simpleTranslation: And our תנא, where does he learn that horses and camels are excluded?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the תנא of our משנה and asks for his source that horses and camels are not included in בכור. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Steps 1–4, the repeated ״פטר חמור״ was used to exclude horses and camels. Our משנה's תנא uses that repetition for a different law: both the mother and the baby must be donkeys. So he needs some other source to exclude horses and camels.

keyTerms.meaning: Our תנא: the author of our משנה
To exclude
Horses and camels
Where does he get it from? (asking for a source)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two opinions. Steps 1–4 showed how רבי יוסי הגלילי uses the double verse. Our משנה's תנא (the רבנן) uses the same double verse for 'both mother and baby must be donkeys,' so he cannot also use it here.

phrases.english: And our Tanna (of the Mishnah),
to exclude horses and camels,
from where does he derive it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא דִידַן, לְמַעוֹטֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים, מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After proving that רבי יוסי הגלילי needs the double verse to exclude horses and camels, the גמרא asks for the other opinion's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source for excluding horses and camels according to the תנא of our משנה, who used the double ״פטר חמור״ for the mother-and-baby law.

steps.title: רב פפא: a general phrase followed by a list limits it to the list
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the verse first gives a general phrase (״כל מקנך״) and then a list (ox, sheep, donkey). By the rule of כלל ופרט, only the listed animals are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: 'All your livestock' is a general statement. 'Ox, sheep, and donkey' is a list of details. When a general statement is followed by details, the general includes only what is in the details. Ox, sheep, and donkey: yes. Anything else: no.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives our משנה's תנא a source: a כלל ופרט reading of the verse in שמות ל״ד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״כל מקנך תזכר״ by itself could cover every animal. But the verse goes on to list ox, sheep, and donkey. The rule כלל ופרט says the general phrase shrinks down to just those listed items, so horses and camels are out.

keyTerms.meaning: 'All your livestock shall be male' (שמות ל״ד:י״ט), the general phrase
A general phrase followed by a list. The general covers only the listed items
The general includes only what is in the list
Anything else

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a second, independent way to exclude horses and camels. It frees the double ״פטר חמור״ for the mother-and-baby law.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
'All your livestock shall be male' is a generalization,
'ox and sheep and donkey' is a detail,
with a generalization and a detail,
the generalization includes only what is in the detail,
ox and sheep and donkey: yes,
anything else: no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כׇּל מִקְנְךָ תִּזָּכָר — כָּלַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A כלל ופרט in the verse limits בכור to ox, sheep, and donkey, which excludes horses and camels.

steps.title: רבי יוסי הגלילי: the word 'firstborn' cuts the donkey off from the list
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יוסי הגלילי does not use רב פפא's כלל ופרט. He answers that the extra word ״פטר״ before ״חמור״ breaks the donkey off from the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי הגלילי? The word 'firstborn' interrupts the topic.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רבי יוסי הגלילי deals with רב פפא's derivation, and answers for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says ״פטר שור ושה ופטר חמור״. Because ״פטר״ is said again, the donkey is a new, separate topic. So the כלל ופרט covers only ox and sheep, and the donkey stands alone. That is why רבי יוסי הגלילי needs the double ״פטר חמור״ to exclude horses and camels.

keyTerms.meaning: Firstborn (literally, 'one that opens the womb')
It interrupted the topic, making a separate section

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili (why doesn't he learn this way)?
The word 'firstborn' interrupted the topic,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the other opinion rejects Step 6's derivation.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי הגלילי's need for the double verse, if כלל ופרט is available
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual reading: the repeated ״פטר״ separates the donkey from the list
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The donkey is part of the list, so כלל ופרט excludes horses and camels.
steps.terutzMaskana: The donkey is a separate topic. The כלל ופרט cannot limit it, so a separate exclusion is needed.

steps.title: The רבנן: the letter ו׳ joins the donkey back in
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן answer that the ו׳ in ״ופטר חמור״ ('and the firstborn') reconnects the donkey to the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? The ו׳ shows that the verse came back and joined it in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the רבנן's reply to רבי יוסי הגלילי's point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Yes, ״פטר״ might seem to start a new topic. But the word begins with ו׳, meaning 'and,' which ties the donkey back to ox and sheep. So the donkey is inside the list, and רב פפא's כלל ופרט works.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages: here, the תנא of our משנה
The letter ו׳, meaning 'and'
The verse came back and mixed it in (connected it)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis (how do they respond)?
The vav ('and') shows the verse went back and combined it.
phrases.notes: The verse says ״ופטר חמור״, and that 'and' links the donkey back to the ox and sheep.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רב פפא's derivation against רבי יוסי הגלילי's claim in Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי הגלילי's claim that ״פטר״ breaks the list
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״פטר״ separates the donkey from the list.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ו׳ joins the donkey back into the list, so כלל ופרט applies.

steps.title: רבי יוסי הגלילי: if the donkey were in the list, both words would be unnecessary
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי הגלילי answers that if the Torah wanted the donkey in the list, it would have written neither the ו׳ nor ״פטר״. Adding both shows separation.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי הגלילי? Let the verse write neither the ו׳ nor 'firstborn.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי הגלילי pushes back against the רבנן's ו׳ argument. The רבנן answer him in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the donkey were meant to be on the list, the Torah could simply have written ״פטר שור ושה חמור״. Adding ״ופטר״ is extra wording, and it shows that a new topic begins. So the ו׳ does not undo the break, and the donkey stays outside the כלל ופרט.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it not write (the Torah could have left it out)

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree horses and camels have no בכור status. They differ on the source. The רבנן use a כלל ופרט, because the ו׳ keeps the donkey in the list. That frees the double ״פטר חמור״ for 'mother and baby both donkeys.' רבי יוסי הגלילי says ״ופטר״ separates the donkey, so he needs the double verse to exclude horses and camels.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili (how does he respond)?
Let it write neither the vav
nor 'firstborn.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי? לָא לִכְתּוֹב לָא וָי״ו וְלָא ״פֶּטֶר״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the רבנן's ו׳ argument from Step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The רבנן's claim that the ו׳ reconnects the donkey to the list
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If the donkey belonged in the list, neither ו׳ nor ״פטר״ was needed. The extra ״ופטר״ shows a separate topic.

steps.title: The רבנן explain why the Torah separates the donkey and then reconnects it
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן answer רבי יוסי הגלילי's challenge. The donkey's holiness is a different type, so the Torah first separates it with ״פטר״ and then joins it back with the ו׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, how do they answer this? Since this one, the donkey, has holiness of value, and that one, the ox and sheep, has holiness of the body, the verse separates them and then joins them back together.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי הגלילי asked why the Torah would write both ״פטר״ and the ו׳ if it wanted the donkey in the list. Here the רבנן answer that question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A firstborn ox or sheep is itself holy and goes on the מזבח. A firstborn donkey is only holy for its money value and gets redeemed with a lamb. So the Torah writes ״פטר״ to show the donkey is a different kind of בכור. Then it writes the ו׳ to show that the donkey is still part of the same list, which limits ״כל מקנך״.

keyTerms.meaning: Holiness of value: the animal's worth is holy, not the animal itself, so it is redeemed
Holiness of the body: the animal itself is holy and is brought as a קרבן
It separates them
It then joins them back together

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן agree that ״פטר״ separates the donkey. But they say the separation only shows that the donkey has a different kind of holiness. The ו׳ still keeps the donkey inside the כלל ופרט list, so horses and camels are left out.
steps.whyThisMatters: This finishes the explanation of how the רבנן know that only ox, sheep, and donkey have בכור status, and not horses or camels.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
Since this one has sanctity of value,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the firstborn donkey, which is redeemed with a lamb.

phrases.english: and that one has inherent (bodily) sanctity —
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the firstborn ox or sheep, which is brought on the altar.

phrases.english: it separates them and then combines them again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יוסי הגלילי's challenge in Step 9 and defends the רבנן's reading of the ו׳ from Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a reason why the Torah writes both the extra word and the joining ו׳
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Writing both ״פטר״ and the ו׳ makes no sense if the donkey belongs in the list, so ״פטר״ must take it out of the list
steps.terutzMaskana: ״פטר״ only shows that the donkey has a different kind of holiness, and the ו׳ keeps it in the list

steps.title: A cow gives birth to a donkey-like calf with some of the cow's features
steps.stepSummary: A new question: if a cow gives birth to a donkey-looking animal that has some of the cow's features, is it a בכור?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: a cow gave birth to a donkey-type animal, and it has some of the cow's features. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a question that has not been decided. The question is about a firstborn that looks like a different species but has some of its mother's features.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already said that a cow that gives birth to a donkey-type animal is not obligated in בכורה. The new point here is the extra detail that the calf has some of the cow's features. The question is whether those features are enough to make it a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked; this introduces a question the חכמים were unsure about
A donkey type; an animal that looks like a donkey
Some of the features, meaning some features of the mother
What is the law?

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
A cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts,
and it has some of the characteristics (of the mother) — what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the verse discussion and starts a new question about a mixed-species birth.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a donkey-like firstborn of a cow, with some of the cow's features, have בכור status?

steps.title: The known case: a goat and a sheep are close enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה's case of a goat and a sheep, where some matching features are enough for בכור status. The reason may be that the two animals are very similar.
steps.simpleTranslation: A goat that gave birth to a sheep-type, or a sheep that gave birth to a goat-type: when it has some features of the mother, it is obligated in בכורה. That may be because this one is kosher and that one is kosher, and this one has holiness of the body and that one has holiness of the body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the question. It brings a known case where the answer is yes, and it points out what makes that case easy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Goats and sheep are both kosher animals. Both of their firstborns are holy in body and go on the מזבח. Because they match in both ways, a few shared features are enough. The question is whether that matching is necessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Obligated in the laws of a firstborn
A kosher animal
A ewe (sheep)

phrases.english: A goat that gave birth to a ewe of sorts,
and a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts,
that when it has some of the characteristics —
it is obligated in firstborn status,
because this is kosher and that is kosher,

phrases.aramaic: הָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף וְהָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף.
phrases.english: this has inherent sanctity and that has inherent sanctity.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֵז שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין רָחֵל, וְרָחֵל שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין עֵז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the question in Step 11 by bringing a known case where the answer is yes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the goat-and-sheep ruling based on how similar the two animals are?

steps.title: Cow and donkey: too different, or both still firstborn animals?
steps.stepSummary: There are two ways to see it. The cow and donkey differ in כשרות and in the kind of holiness they have, so maybe the calf is not a בכור. Or maybe it is, since both species are covered by the laws of בכורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But here, this one is non-kosher and that one is kosher, and this one has holiness of the body while that one has holiness of value. So maybe it is not holy. Or perhaps, since both of them become holy as a בכור, it is holy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out both sides of the question. One side says the calf is not holy because the two species are too different. The other side says it is holy because both species have בכור status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one says the goat-and-sheep ruling only works when the two animals match. A cow and a donkey do not match: the cow is kosher and holy in body, while the donkey is non-kosher and holy only in value. Side two says matching does not matter, because the only thing needed is that both species are part of the בכורה laws. Steps 17 and 19 later read the ברייתות as saying that this cow-and-donkey calf, when it has some of the mother's features, is a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-kosher animal
Or perhaps; this introduces the other side of a question
This one and that one; both
Able to become holy as a firstborn

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that the donkey has no holiness at all. A firstborn donkey is a real בכור. Its holiness is just a different type: it is holy for its value and is redeemed, instead of going on the מזבח.
steps.whatToRemember: The question is this: does a mixed-species firstborn need its mother and its own species to match fully, both kosher and both holy in body? Or is it enough that both species are covered by the בכורה laws?

phrases.english: Here, where this is non-kosher and that is kosher,

phrases.aramaic: הָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף וְהָא קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים — לָא,
phrases.english: this has inherent sanctity and that has sanctity of value — perhaps not,
or perhaps:
since both this one and that one
are subject to firstborn sanctity — it is sanctified?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the cow-and-donkey case with the goat-and-sheep case from Step 12 and gives both sides of the question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is full matching between the species needed, or is it enough that both are covered by the בכורה laws?

steps.title: What if a donkey gives birth to a horse-like foal?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose a cow's donkey-like calf is a בכור because both animals have בכורה. Then what about a donkey that gives birth to a horse-like foal?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that since both this one and that one are covered by בכורה, the newborn is holy, what about a donkey that gave birth to a kind of horse? Here a horse is certainly not covered by בכורה. Or perhaps, since it is a non-kosher species like its mother, it is holy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא climbs one step higher in its chain of questions. It assumes one answer to the last question and asks a harder case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the cow-and-donkey case, both species are covered by בכורה. A horse is never covered by בכורה, so that reason is gone. But the donkey and the horse are both non-kosher (טמאה), so maybe that similarity is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say: assume one answer to the earlier question and move on to a new one
This one and that one, meaning both
Becomes holy with בכור status
A kind of horse, a horse-like newborn
A non-kosher species

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. It is a 'ladder' of questions. Each rung assumes the answer to the rung below it, so you must keep the earlier cow-and-donkey question in mind.

phrases.english: And if you say:
since both this one and that one
are made holy with firstborn status, it is holy,
phrases.notes: This takes for granted the 'yes' answer to the cow-and-donkey question from Step 13.

phrases.english: a donkey that gave birth to a kind of horse, what is the law?
Here certainly it is not something that becomes holy
with firstborn status,
or perhaps
since it is a non-kosher species, it is holy?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assumes the 'it is a בכור' side of Step 13 and asks the next, harder case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a donkey's horse-like foal that shares some of its mother's features count as a בכור, given that horses have no בכורה but both animals are non-kosher?

steps.title: What if a cow gives birth to a horse-like calf?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the donkey's horse-like foal is a בכור. Then what about a cow that gives birth to a horse-like calf? Here the two animals share nothing, unless the shared features alone are enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that since it is a non-kosher species it is holy, what about a cow that gave birth to a kind of horse? Here this one is kosher and that one is non-kosher. This one is covered by בכורה and that one is not. Or perhaps the shared features are what really matter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא climbs to the top rung of the ladder. It asks about the case where mother and newborn have the least in common.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both earlier reasons fail here. A cow is kosher and a horse is not, and a cow has בכורה while a horse does not. The only remaining reason is that the newborn shares some of its mother's features (סימנין). Maybe that is enough by itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Kosher (an animal)
Identifying features or signs of the mother seen in the newborn
Is something significant, it counts

steps.whyThisMatters: This case tests whether shared features alone can create בכור status, with no help from any other similarity between the species.

phrases.english: If you say:
since it is a non-kosher species it is holy,
a cow that gave birth to a kind of horse, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא וַדַּאי הָא טְהוֹרָה וְהָא טְמֵאָה,
phrases.english: Here certainly this one is kosher and that one is non-kosher,
this one becomes holy with firstborn status
and that one does not become holy with firstborn status,
or perhaps the features are what count?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assumes the 'holy' side of Step 14 and asks the most extreme case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can shared features alone make a cow's horse-like calf a בכור, even though the species differ in both כשרות and בכורה?

steps.title: Proof attempt from a general ברייתא about kosher animals
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says a kosher animal's non-kosher-looking newborn is a בכור if it has some of the mother's features. The גמרא suggests this even includes a cow that gives birth to a horse-like calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A kosher animal that gave birth to a kind of non-kosher animal is exempt from בכורה. If the newborn has some of the mother's features, it is obligated in בכורה. Doesn't this include even a cow that gave birth to a kind of horse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to answer the cow-and-horse question from Step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא speaks broadly about any non-kosher kind, without naming which one. Since the wording is general, the גמרא suggests it covers a horse too. That would mean shared features alone are enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt from the laws of בכורה
Some of the features
Obligated in the laws of בכורה
Isn't it so that…? A suggested reading of the source

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: בְּהֵמָה טְהוֹרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה —
phrases.english: a kosher animal that gave birth to a kind of non-kosher animal
is exempt from firstborn status;
if it has some of the features,
it is obligated in firstborn status.
Isn't it so that this includes even
a cow that gave birth to a kind of horse?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of Step 15.
steps.raayaObject: That a cow's horse-like calf with some of the mother's features is a בכור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that uses the general phrase 'a kind of non-kosher animal'.

steps.title: The ברייתא means a donkey-like calf
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The ברייתא may only be talking about a cow that gives birth to a donkey-like calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means a cow that gave birth to a kind of donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof by reading the ברייתא more narrowly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A donkey, unlike a horse, is covered by בכורה. So the ברייתא may only teach the easier cow-and-donkey case. The cow-and-horse question stays open, but this reading suggests the cow-and-donkey calf is a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: A kind of donkey, a donkey-like newborn

phrases.english: No,
it means a cow that gave birth to a kind of donkey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof only. The cow-and-horse question remains unanswered.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The general wording of the ברייתא can be limited to a non-kosher kind that is covered by בכורה, such as a donkey.

steps.title: Proof attempt from a ברייתא that lists two cases
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא lists a cow with a donkey-like calf and a donkey with a horse-like foal. It says either is a בכור if it has some features. The גמרא suggests this last line applies to both cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A cow that gave birth to a kind of donkey, and a donkey that gave birth to a kind of horse, is exempt from בכורה. If it has some of the features, it is obligated in בכורה. Doesn't this go on both cases?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא to answer the donkey-and-horse question from Step 14, and also the cow-and-donkey question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא names the donkey-and-horse case directly. If the line about features applies to both cases it lists, then a donkey's horse-like foal is a בכור. That would answer Step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: On both of them, meaning the rule applies to both cases

phrases.english: Come and hear:
a cow that gave birth to a kind of donkey,
and a donkey that gave birth to a kind of horse
is exempt from firstborn status;
if it has some of the features,
it is obligated in firstborn status.
Isn't it so that this applies to both?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the cow-and-horse proof fails, the גמרא tries to answer the donkey-and-horse question of Step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That a donkey's horse-like foal with some of the mother's features is a בכור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that explicitly lists the donkey-and-horse case next to the cow-and-donkey case.

steps.title: The features rule only goes on the cow case
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The line about some features may only apply to the cow that gives birth to a donkey-like calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it goes on the cow that gave birth to a kind of donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the second proof. The rule about features does not have to apply to both cases the ברייתא lists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'some features' line may refer only to the first case, the cow and donkey. The donkey-and-horse question from Step 14, and so also the cow-and-horse question, is left without a proof. Only the cow-and-donkey case is shown to be a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: No (Aramaic), used to reject a proof

steps.whatToRemember: Neither ברייתא settles the horse cases. Both proofs are limited to a cow with a donkey-like calf, which the ברייתות show is a בכור if it has some of the mother's features.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא mentions the donkey-and-horse case, but that does not prove it gets the 'some features' rule. The גמרא reads that rule as going only on the first case.

phrases.english: No,
it applies to a cow that gave birth to a kind of donkey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof for the donkey-and-horse case. The cow-and-donkey case is answered.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The final clause of the ברייתא can be read as applying only to its first case, not to both.

steps.title: Why list the donkey with a horse-like foal at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the 'some features' line covers only the cow case, why does the ברייתא mention the donkey with a horse-like foal? If it is to say the foal is not a בכור, that is obvious from a קל וחומר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, the case of a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal: why does the ברייתא teach it? To say it is exempt? That is obvious! Think about it. A cow and a donkey are both animals that have בכור status. Yet with a cow that gave birth to a donkey-like calf, you said the calf counts only if it has some of the mother's features, and otherwise it does not. Then with a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal, do we even need to say it is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the reading from the last step and now attacks it. If the ברייתא lists the donkey-horse case only to exempt it, that case seems to teach nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cows and donkeys are both animals that can have בכור status. Even so, a cow's donkey-like calf needs some of the mother's features to count. A horse is not an animal that has בכור status at all, so by קל וחומר the donkey's horse-like foal should surely be exempt. Then why would the ברייתא bother listing it?

keyTerms.meaning: For what purpose does it teach this?
To exempt it (to say it is not a בכור)
It's obvious!
Now, if even… (opens a קל וחומר)
Animals that can have בכור status
Is it even necessary to say?

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two animals here. A donkey does have בכור status (פטר חמור), but a horse does not. That is why the cow-donkey case is the stronger case for the קל וחומר.

phrases.english: But a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal,
for what purpose does it teach it?
To exempt it? That is obvious!

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא, וּמָה פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר,
phrases.english: Now, if a cow that gave birth to a donkey-like calf,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בְּנֵי מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה נִינְהוּ,
phrases.english: where both this and that are animals that can have firstborn status,

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרַתְּ: אִם יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְצָת סִימָנִין — אִין,
phrases.english: you said: if it has some of the features, yes,
and if not, no,
then a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal, is it necessary to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the reading from Step 19 and challenges what follows from it: the donkey-horse case now seems to add nothing.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's listing of the donkey-horse case, under the reading of Step 19.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from the cow-donkey case, where both animals have בכור status, makes the exemption of a donkey's horse-like foal obvious. A case that teaches nothing new should not be listed.

steps.title: Needed because the foal might seem to be just a red donkey
steps.stepSummary: The case was needed. A cow and a donkey look very different, but a donkey and a horse look alike. So we might have thought the foal is just a red donkey and counts as a בכור. The ברייתא tells us it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was necessary. You might have thought this: there, in the cow case, one animal has horns and the other has none, and one has split hooves while the other has closed hooves. But here, neither the donkey nor the horse has horns, and both have closed hooves. So I might say the foal is simply a red donkey. The ברייתא teaches us that it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The donkey-horse case teaches something new that the cow case could not teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קל וחומר assumed the cow case is the stronger one. But the cow case had a weakness: a cow and a donkey look completely different, which is exactly why the calf might not count. A donkey and a horse share horn-lessness and closed hooves, so we might have said the foal is really a donkey of a different color and is a בכור. The ברייתא rules that out.

keyTerms.meaning: It was necessary (to teach this)
It would have entered your mind (you might have thought)
Horns
Split hooves / closed, uncloven hooves
Merely a red donkey (a donkey with a horse's coloring)
It teaches us (otherwise)

steps.whatToRemember: A קל וחומר can fail when the 'weaker' case has its own reason to be more lenient. Here, the strong physical likeness between a donkey and a horse could have made us call the foal a donkey. So the ברייתא needed to list the donkey-horse case separately.

phrases.english: It was necessary, because it would enter your mind:
there, it is so because this one has horns,
and that one has no horns;
this one's hooves are split,
and that one's hooves are closed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי אֵין לָהּ קַרְנַיִם,
phrases.english: But here, where both this one and that one have no horns,
and both this one and that one have closed hooves,
I might say it is merely a red donkey,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 20 by showing the donkey-horse case teaches something the cow case cannot.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing the extra case is necessary because it has its own reason for a different conclusion.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a donkey and a horse share key physical features, the foal is really a red donkey and counts as a בכור.
steps.terutzMaskana: The foal is a different species from its mother. It is not a בכור just because the two animals look alike in general.

steps.title: Why does the משנה add 'because that which emerges'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule about eating offspring that look like another species. It asks why the משנה needs to add the reason, 'because that which emerges.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And what is their status regarding eating, etc.' Why do I need the משנה to teach the words 'because that which emerges'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה, the rule about eating such offspring. It asks why the משנה adds an explanation that seems unnecessary, which sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already rules that a kosher animal's unusual-looking offspring may be eaten and a non-kosher animal's may not. Adding 'because what emerges from the non-kosher is non-kosher, and from the kosher is kosher' looks like a repeat. The גמרא wants to know what this extra phrase teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Regarding eating (whether it is kosher to eat)
Etc. (the quote of the משנה continues)
Why do I need it to teach?
'Because that which emerges' (from the animal)

phrases.english: "And what is their status regarding eating, etc."
Why do I need it to teach "because that which emerges"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the בכור discussion and opens a new topic in the משנה: the rule about eating.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra point the משנה's phrase 'because that which emerges' teaches, beyond the ruling it already gave.

steps.title: The added reason is only a memory aid: follow the mother
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's phrase 'because that which emerges...' teaches no new law. It is a memory aid so we do not reverse the rule. We follow the mother, not the offspring's appearance.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is just a memory aid, so you will not mix things up. Do not say, 'Go by the animal's own looks, so this one is fully kosher and that one is fully non-kosher.' Rather, go by its mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 22. The extra reason in the משנה is only a memory aid that keeps us from flipping the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think an offspring's status depends on what it looks like. A kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother would then be fully טהור. The משנה's phrasing reminds us that the deciding factor is always the mother.

keyTerms.meaning: A sign or memory aid
Merely, just
Get mixed up, get reversed
Full-fledged, completely
Go after its mother (follow the mother's status)

steps.whatToRemember: An animal's kosher status follows its mother, not its own appearance.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the offspring's looks decide its status. A kosher-looking calf of a non-kosher mother is forbidden. A non-kosher-looking calf of a kosher mother is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule, 'follow the mother.' The next steps look for the verse that teaches it.

phrases.english: It is merely a mnemonic,
so that you do not get it reversed,
so that you do not say: follow its own appearance,
and this one (kosher-looking) is a full-fledged kosher animal,
and that one (non-kosher-looking) is a full-fledged non-kosher animal,
rather, follow its mother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 22 about why the משנה adds the reason 'because that which emerges.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The added phrase is a memory aid, so we do not reverse the rule and judge by appearance. We follow the mother.

steps.title: Asking for the source of the rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we learn that an animal's status follows its mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the Torah source of the 'follow the mother' rule. This is a setup line that leads into the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the rule is clear, the גמרא wants a verse behind it. This opens a new search for a source.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these matters derived? (a request for a source)

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining the rule in Step 23, the גמרא asks for its scriptural source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The verse that teaches that an animal's status follows its mother.

steps.title: The verse teaches a kosher-looking animal from a non-kosher mother is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads 'אך את זה לא תאכלו ממעלי הגרה וממפריסי הפרסה' as hinting at an animal with both kosher signs that is still forbidden. That animal is a kosher-looking one born from a non-kosher mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught: 'But this you shall not eat, from those that chew the cud and from those that split the hoof.' This means there is an animal that chews the cud and has split hooves, yet you may not eat it. Which is it? A kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question with a ברייתא. The ברייתא learns from a verse that a kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother may not be eaten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse seems to say that some animals with kosher signs are still forbidden. Normally, both signs make an animal kosher. So there must be a special case, and the ברייתא says it is the kosher-looking offspring of a non-kosher mother. This fits the rule of following the mother.

keyTerms.meaning: Chews the cud (a kosher sign)
Has split hooves (a kosher sign)
A kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher animal

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
"Nevertheless, this you shall not eat
of those that chew the cud and of those that split the hoof" —

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ לְךָ שֶׁהוּא מַעֲלֵה גֵרָה וּמַפְרִיס פַּרְסָה
phrases.english: you have an animal that chews the cud and has split hooves
and yet you may not eat it.
And which is this?
A kosher animal that was born from a non-kosher one.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן: אַךְ אֶת זֶה לֹא תֹאכְלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 24's request for a source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse 'אך את זה לא תאכלו ממעלי הגרה' refers to a kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother, which is forbidden.

steps.title: Maybe the verse means a non-kosher-looking animal from a kosher mother
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests another reading. Perhaps the verse forbids a non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher mother. If so, it asks how to explain the words 'ממעלי הגרה וממפריסי הפרסה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps it means only a non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher one. And if so, what does 'of those that chew the cud and of those that split the hoof' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tests its own reading by suggesting the opposite case. This is a setup line: it leads into the explanation of the verse's words that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opposite reading would forbid a non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher mother. That would contradict the 'follow the mother' rule. The ברייתא asks how this reading would fit the words 'of those that chew the cud,' since this offspring has no kosher signs itself. The ברייתא continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps it is only... (introduces an alternative reading)
A non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher animal

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the final ruling. The ברייתא is only testing an alternative reading of the verse, and it will reject it.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טָמֵא הַנּוֹלָד מִן הַטָּהוֹר,
phrases.english: Or perhaps it refers only to a non-kosher animal born from a kosher one,
and then what is meant by "of those that chew the cud and of those that split the hoof"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טָמֵא הַנּוֹלָד מִן הַטָּהוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 25's reading of the verse by suggesting the opposite case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's reading that the verse forbids a kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse might instead forbid a non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher mother. That raises the question of how to explain the words 'ממעלי הגרה.'
